morning.text: Morning! You'll never guess. Mrs Lowe's Jack came in on the 9.40 this morning. She was on the platform, waiting. Cried her eyes out, the pair of them.
Funny thing. Mrs Lowe was on Platform 9 all yesterday morning with a photograph, waiting for the 9.40. Her Jack came in today. She'd gone home by then. Worn out, poor love.
And look what turned up off Platform 9 last night. A little velvet box. It's in drawer A. It's... humming.

My lamp's yours now, love. Switch on the blue bulb (press L while you're holding something) and you'll see what ink tries to hide.

Every Ninefold ticket has its date in blue.

intro.text: Mornin'! Big Sid. Platelayer. I've lost me {dinner|tin}.
Tin box, red. {Corned beef doorstep in it|sandwich}. Left it in the hut on Tuesday and some article's moved it.
{My Mavis always puts a note in|note}. Don't tell the lads. I'll never hear the end of it.

claims.text: A note from his wife, Mavis

answers.text: Corned beef. Thick as a sleeper. That's Mavis.
"Ask about the raise." Oh, Mavis. I'll ask. I'll ask today.

verdicts.ledger: The corned beef and Mavis's note. Sid got his dinner back, and asked about the raise.

reply.text: Lovely jubbly! Right. The raise. Here goes nothing.

verdicts.ledger: Mavis's note was right there inside. It was Sid's.

reply.text: Me dinner, though!

verdicts.ledger: Corned beef is many things, but not uncanny. It should have gone home.

reply.text: You've locked up me sandwich. That's cruel, that is.

intro.text: Thursday, as promised. I've come for {the ring|ring}. Gold. {"A, always the 9:40, T" inside the band|engraving}.
Mrs Pell held it for me. For years. There's her chit, in her own hand. You know her hand, don't you?
She'd want you to honour it. Family should honour family.

claims.text: A gold ring in a velvet box
"A, always the 9:40, T" inside the band

answers.text: "A, always the 9:40, T." Romantic, isn't it? Wasted on them.
The 9.40. Everyone was on the 9.40, that morning.
1921. A good year for me. Things were lost.

verdicts.ledger: Mr Vell knew the engraving and brought a chit in Agnes's hand. Under the blue lamp it said NEVER TO VELL. The Grey Gentleman gets nothing.

reply.text: No. Of course. She always did say no.
Tomorrow, then. I'll bring the proper paperwork. For the drawer itself.

verdicts.ledger: You kept the ring from Mr Vell. But it wasn't from tomorrow: it was from 1921, waiting for its owner. Now it's in the Iron Drawer.

reply.text: The Iron Drawer. Where nobody gets it. That will do nicely, actually.

verdicts.ledger: You gave the Grey Gentleman Agnes's ring. The chit said NEVER TO VELL, in blue.

reply.text: Thank you.
Forty-one years she waited for this. And you just... handed it over.

intro.text: Vernon Spratt, violinist. That's {my violin case|case}. Black, fiddle-shaped. I left it at the Railway Arms on Tuesday night.
{My name's on the label inside: V. Spratt|label}. Clear as day.
Hey now. That's {my fiddle|case}, friend. Mmm. I think.
It was a long night. Real long. There's a... {a list? Songs? Taped in there somewhere|setlist}.
You hear that? She's singing. She always sings when I'm close.

claims.text: A list of songs taped in it somewhere

answers.text: V. Spratt. In the f-hole. Look for yourself.
Delacroix. New Orleans. My granddaddy put it there.
Last Train Home, always first. Then the Blues. Then Mabel's Waltz, for the old folks.

notMine.text: That ain't her. She's a fiddle.

verdicts.ledger: Lou's story was foggy, but the case hummed the moment he spoke, and the label said Delacroix. If it hums, it's home.

reply.text: There's my girl. Come to Lou.
Worth a try.

verdicts.ledger: It hummed for Lou, not Spratt, and the label said L. Delacroix.

reply.text: Ha! Thank you kindly.
...She's crying, man. Can't you hear her?

verdicts.ledger: It hummed for Lou. Things that hum know their owners.

reply.text: Aw, now. She's right there.

verdicts.ledger: A humming violin is recognition, not danger. It should have gone home with Lou.

reply.text: You locked up my girl? Man.

intro.text: Darling! Edie Larkspur. You've seen my Viola, of course. Everyone has.
I've lost {a gramophone record|record}. {Lou's band|label}. He gave it to me. He hasn't yet, but he will, I can feel it.
It came to the stage door by mistake and the doorman sent it here. Hand it over, there's a lamb.

answers.text: Lou Delacroix and the Ninefold Five. "Last Train Home." He's going to be enormous.
March? Darling, it's October. Oh. Oh!

notMine.text: Darling, no. A record. Round. Black.

verdicts.ledger: It was Edie's (or will be). But the sleeve said recorded March 1963. Tomorrow can mean next year. Into the Iron Drawer.

reply.text: March! Then I shall simply have to wait for it. How thrilling.

verdicts.ledger: The sleeve said March 1963. It came from tomorrow: it should have gone in the Iron Drawer.

reply.text: Divine! I shall play it until the needle wears through.

verdicts.ledger: Right not to hand it over. But a record from next year belongs in the Iron Drawer.

reply.text: Refused! Me! Well, I never.

intro.text: Hello again, miss. I said I'd come back. I'm looking for {a ring|ring}, in a little velvet box.
It's engraved. {"A, always the 9:40, T."|engraving} A for Agnes. That's her name.
I dropped it on {the 9.40 to Harwick, Friday the fourteenth of October|when}. Nineteen twenty-one.
Can you hear that? Is that... is that it?

claims.text: A ring in a little velvet box

answers.text: A for Agnes. T for Thomas. Always the 9.40, because that's where I first saw her.
First class. I'd saved for weeks. I wanted to arrive properly.
The fourteenth of October, 1921. The day I meant to ask her.

notMine.text: No, miss. The little velvet box. Can't you hear it?

missing.text: Gone? To a gentleman in grey?
Locked away? Where nobody can reach it?
Then I'll keep looking. I'm good at looking. I've had a lot of practice.

cases.missingLedger: Thomas came back for the ring, but it was gone.

verdicts.ledger: It hummed for Thomas. The engraving, the 1921 ticket, the date under the lamp: everything matched. After forty-one years, the ring went home.

reply.text: Oh.
Thank you, miss. Thank you. I'd best not keep her waiting. Not any longer.

verdicts.ledger: It hummed the moment Thomas spoke. It was his. It was always his.

reply.text: But it's singing. It knows me.
I'll keep waiting, then. One of us always is.

verdicts.ledger: It wasn't from tomorrow. It was from 1921, and its owner had come for it.

reply.text: Locked away. So close.

evening.text: That's Mr Hale. The old Station Master. Agnes's Tom. They were married forty-one years. I went to the party!
Long day. That young fellow in the old suit went away without his ring. Looked like he'd been waiting a long time.
Mr Vell was outside the barrier when I locked up. Just standing. Says he'll be in tomorrow, with paperwork.

gazette.headline: STATION MASTER'S WIDOW... NO, WAIT
gazette.body: Correction: in yesterday's edition the Gazette reported that Mr Thomas Hale, Station Master at Ninefold from 1930 to 1961, had died in 1921. The Gazette apologises. Mr and Mrs Hale will celebrate forty-one years of marriage this Sunday.

gazette.headline: STATION CLOCKS STOP AT 9.40
gazette.body: Every clock at Ninefold Junction stopped at twenty to ten yesterday morning, and was found to be running backwards by the afternoon. Station staff describe the platforms as "greyer, somehow".

gazette.headline: MISS LARKSPUR TO RECORD WITH BANDLEADER
gazette.body: Actress Edie Larkspur has denied rumours of a recording with jazz violinist Lou Delacroix. "Not until March, darling," she told the Gazette, and then appeared surprised at herself.
